title: Employee Share Options: What to Ask Payroll
content:
Before exercising employee share options in Kenya, get a written payroll calculation showing the award type, valuation date, benefit amount and how any tax will be funded. An offer described as “shares” may give you options, actual shares or a cash payment linked to a share price. Those descriptions should not be treated as interchangeable.

The PAYE calculator helps you check your ordinary salary baseline. It does not value an option, establish the tax event for your plan or calculate tax on a later share disposal.

First identify what the award actually gives you

Ask HR or the plan administrator for the signed award agreement and plan rules. An option generally gives you a right to acquire shares at an agreed price, subject to its conditions. A vesting schedule describes when conditions are satisfied; exercise is the step where you use the option. A later sale is another transaction.

Write down the grant date, vesting dates, exercise deadline, exercise price, currency, number of options and the company issuing the shares. Confirm what happens to unvested and vested awards if you leave. Do not count an unexercised option as money available for rent or other monthly spending; use the broader salary-versus-benefits comparison when assessing the offer.

Ask which valuation rule and date payroll is applying

The enacted Finance Act 2023, section 5(b) changed the share-option valuation reference in section 5(6)(c) of the Income Tax Act from grant to exercise. That amendment is a reason to question a worksheet that automatically uses the old grant-date price. It is not a substitute for identifying the rules applicable to your particular award.

Request a worksheet with the number of shares, employee purchase price, market-value evidence, valuation date and any currency conversion. For an unlisted company, ask who prepared the valuation and what document supports it. For an overseas plan, ask the Kenyan payroll team to confirm the local treatment rather than relying only on the parent company's foreign tax summary.

KRA's PAYE guidance explains that employment income can include non-cash benefits. The fact that no cash arrived in your bank account does not by itself settle the payroll treatment. Our benefits-in-kind guide explains why a taxable benefit and cash salary can differ.

Worked example: separate purchase cost from benefit

Assume, solely for illustration, that payroll confirms an applicable value of KES 120 per share and an employee purchase price of KES 80 for 1,000 shares.

  • Cash purchase cost: 1,000 × KES 80 = KES 80,000.
  • Assumed share value: 1,000 × KES 120 = KES 120,000.
  • Difference to assess under the applicable rules: KES 40,000.

The KES 40,000 difference is not a KES 40,000 tax bill. Nor is the KES 80,000 purchase cost the tax. Before committing cash, ask payroll for the actual tax calculation and how much will be withheld from salary, collected separately or funded through an authorised share sale. Do not assume shares can immediately be sold: check the plan's dealing restrictions and whether a buyer exists.

Does the employer say tax is deferred?

Section 5(c) of the Finance Act 2023 introduced a specific deferred-tax framework for qualifying eligible-start-up shares issued instead of cash emoluments. Ask payroll to identify the legal provision, show why both the employer and award qualify, and specify the events that end deferral. “We are a start-up” is not sufficient evidence, and that framework should not be assumed to cover every share-option plan.

If deferral is claimed, get the monitoring responsibility and payment timetable in writing, including what happens on leaving employment. Keep this confirmation with the award documents so it is available even after your work account closes.

Before you approve exercise

  • Resolve any difference between the administrator's and payroll's share counts.
  • Obtain the valuation evidence and the expected payroll period.
  • Confirm both purchase funding and tax funding.
  • Keep the exercise confirmation and subsequent payslip; ask how the benefit will be reflected in your annual payroll records.
  • Get separate advice on a later disposal or cross-border allocation if relevant; a payroll calculation does not answer every investment-tax question.

Employers can use the employer payroll guide to place these records alongside the rest of their payroll controls.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 7 November 2026 using KRA's PAYE guidance and the Finance Act 2023 linked above. Legislative references describe enacted provisions; plan-specific eligibility, valuation and timing still require confirmation.

title: Reconcile Your Mortgage Interest Certificate
content:
To reconcile a mortgage interest certificate, compare the lender's interest figure with the interest supported by your account statements and the deduction already allowed through payroll. Your mortgage instalment, interest paid and tax saving are three different numbers.

Use the mortgage relief calculator to estimate the effect of qualifying interest after checking the underlying documents. For the eligibility rules, start with claiming mortgage interest relief in Kenya; this article focuses on finding and resolving differences in the records.

Check the certificate's identity and period

Confirm the borrower name, loan account, property reference and covered year. Check whether the document is provisional or final, and retain the issue date. If a lender replaces a certificate, keep the replacement and a note explaining which earlier version it supersedes. Do not add both versions together.

Ask for a transaction statement if the certificate shows only an annual total. A repayment schedule prepared when the mortgage began is useful for planning, but rate changes, payment changes or loan settlement can make it differ from what actually happened.

Separate interest from the total repayment

KRA's current PAYE guidance allows qualifying mortgage interest up to KES 360,000 annually, or KES 30,000 monthly. It requires borrowing from an institution within the first six categories in the Income Tax Act's Fourth Schedule to buy or improve a residence occupied by the borrower.

A certificate alone does not prove every eligibility condition. Confirm the lender, loan purpose and occupation evidence as well. Keep principal repayments, insurance premiums and administrative charges separate rather than copying the entire bank debit into the interest field. Where a statement includes reversals or interest adjustments, ask the lender how those entries affect the certified figure.

Build a month-by-month reconciliation

A simple spreadsheet or handwritten schedule can use these columns:

  • Month: include every month, even if the interest or payroll deduction is zero.
  • Lender interest: record the supported interest amount and statement reference.
  • Payroll deduction: record the mortgage-interest amount actually used to reduce taxable pay, not the repayment taken from your bank account.
  • Difference: subtract payroll's amount from the lender-supported eligible amount, then explain the gap.
  • Action: identify whether the lender, payroll team or you must supply evidence.

Apply the relevant limit and eligibility checks before treating the difference as an omitted deduction. Do not simply spread a large annual amount equally across months or treat a positive difference as an automatic refund. The tax relief and deductions guide explains the broader distinction between reducing taxable income and reducing tax itself.

Worked example: payroll used an estimate

Assume a qualifying loan, a full year of eligibility and no complicating adjustments. Payroll used KES 25,000 a month, while the lender's final records show KES 23,000 of qualifying interest in each month.

  • Payroll total: 12 × KES 25,000 = KES 300,000.
  • Supported interest: 12 × KES 23,000 = KES 276,000.
  • Deduction difference: KES 24,000 too much used in the illustrative payroll calculation.

Both totals are below the annual ceiling, yet the difference still matters: a ceiling does not replace evidence of actual qualifying interest. KES 24,000 is the deduction discrepancy, not the resulting tax payable. Payroll must calculate the tax consequences using the complete relevant figures.

Match the result to payslips and your P9

Add the mortgage deductions shown across your payslips and compare them with your annual payroll certificate. If you changed jobs, collect records from both employers and check for overlapping months. Our P9-to-payslip checklist helps locate payroll discrepancies without confusing them with lender errors.

If payroll already allowed the correct interest, entering the same supported deduction in an annual reconciliation must not produce a second deduction on top of it. Trace the figures before submitting or amending a return. If the year is still running, send corrected evidence promptly rather than allowing an inaccurate estimate to continue.

Resolve the difference with the right organisation

Ask the lender to explain a certificate that disagrees with its transaction history. Ask payroll to explain or correct the amount it used after you supply the confirmed evidence. KRA's guidance on employers applying deductions and reliefs stresses supporting documentation. Use the PAYE tax-relief document checklist to keep the certificate, loan evidence and correction trail together.

If a discrepancy remains when you need to file, obtain clarification from KRA or a qualified adviser with the actual records. Neither a new certificate nor a calculator result guarantees a refund.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 7 November 2026 against the KRA PAYE and employer-deduction guidance linked above. All worked figures are illustrative, not an assessment of an individual mortgage.

title: Payroll Bank Details: Safe Changes and Failed Payments
featuredImageAlt: Payroll clerk reviewing a plain form beside a closed laptop and phone
metaTitle: Payroll Bank Details: Safe Changes and Failed Payments
metaDescription: Change payroll bank details safely in Kenya, confirm the effective month and trace a failed salary payment without creating a duplicate transfer.
content:
Change salary-payment details through your employer's approved private process, obtain confirmation of the payroll period affected and check the first payment. If salary does not arrive, establish whether the instruction was never submitted, rejected, returned or sent to the wrong destination before requesting another transfer.

Use the PAYE calculator to check the expected salary calculation. It cannot trace a bank transfer: a correct net-pay figure and a successful payment are separate checks.

Submit a clear change request

Ask payroll which secure channel and evidence it accepts. Supply the account-holder name, bank and account information required by that process, plus the intended effective month. Do not send passwords, PINs or one-time codes. A colleague should not need access to your banking login to update the employer's payment instructions.

Section 17 of the Employment Act includes payment into a bank or building-society account designated by the employee. Ask payroll to retain your designation and verify any subsequent change independently. The steps here are recommended controls, not a prescribed universal bank form.

For employers, a second reviewer should compare the approved instruction with the payroll master record. Confirm unexpected changes using contact details already held on file rather than a new phone number supplied in the change message. Keep a record of who checked the request and when it became effective.

Confirm which payment will use the new account

A request arriving after a payroll file is prepared may need separate handling. Ask whether the file has already been released and which account will receive that month's pay. Do not close the old account solely because you sent an email requesting a change.

A useful confirmation records the effective payroll month, masked account ending and whether any payment remains in progress. Keep the acknowledgement privately. The new employee payroll checklist covers initial setup; this workflow is for a later change or failed payment.

Trace a missing credit without duplicating salary

Compare the payslip's net amount with actual credits. Send payroll the period, expected amount and payment date, asking for a transaction reference and confirmed status. Share only the relevant part of a bank record, through the approved channel.

If payroll says the bank rejected or returned the payment, ask for the rejection reason and the proposed correction. If it reports successful payment, ask the bank to trace that reference. A screenshot showing a payment instruction is not the same evidence as confirmation of its final status.

For example, if net salary is KES 70,000 and a KES 70,000 transfer is returned, a replacement KES 70,000 settles the original amount; it does not represent KES 140,000 earned. Keep the original, return and replacement references together. If both transfers arrive, tell payroll promptly and follow the salary-overpayment reconciliation process.

Close the issue with evidence

Record the actual credit date and amount. Confirm that future payments use the correct account and that no duplicate salary or recovery has been entered. Ask payroll separately about any tax-record adjustment rather than changing figures yourself merely because a transfer failed.

If salary remains unpaid, preserve the communications and seek advice from a labour officer, union or qualified adviser on the appropriate route. The employment situations guide helps distinguish payment problems from disputed deductions or pay entitlements.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 10 November 2026. Employment Act sections 17 support the legal points above. The practical checklists are editorial guidance; examples are illustrative.

title: How to Check a Certificate of Service in Kenya
featuredImageAlt: Employee receiving a cream document folder from an HR colleague at an office doorway
metaTitle: How to Check a Certificate of Service in Kenya
metaDescription: Check a Kenyan certificate of service: required particulars, employment dates, corrections and how it differs from a reference, P9 or final-pay statement.
content:
A certificate of service records your employment history. Check the employer, your name, employment dates, work description and usual workplace before filing it away. It is different from a reference, a final-pay statement and your P9 tax certificate.

If you are also checking final ordinary salary, use the PAYE calculator. It does not establish a certificate entitlement or calculate every item in a termination settlement. The employment situations guide connects the separate exit checks.

Who should receive a certificate?

Section 51 of the Employment Act requires an employer to issue a certificate on termination, except where employment lasted less than four consecutive weeks. The same section distinguishes that certificate from a testimonial or performance reference, which the employer is not generally bound to provide under that provision.

Ask for a certificate of service specifically. A request for a “recommendation letter” can be interpreted as a request for an assessment of your performance rather than the factual document you need.

Check the statutory particulars

The section lists the employer's name and postal address, the employee's name, commencement date, nature and usual place of employment, cessation date and any other prescribed particulars. Compare these against your employment records rather than relying on memory.

Check a misspelt name against your onboarding records. Compare the start date with the appointment documents and the cessation date with the exit correspondence. A last day physically in the office can differ from the end of employment; ask HR to explain the date used where notice or leave creates a difference.

For someone who moved between roles, ask whether the description accurately records the work. Do not assume a new job title means a new start date. If the employing company changed, ask HR which employer and period the document covers instead of combining records without explanation.

Keep it separate from the money documents

A certificate of service does not show whether all final salary, leave or notice amounts were paid. Use the employee exit payroll checklist for that calculation and payment trail.

Likewise, it does not replace the tax figures needed to check a P9 against payslips. Maintain a small exit folder with distinct documents for employment history, final-pay calculation, payment evidence and tax records. One document cannot reliably answer all four questions.

Request a correction without altering the original

Send HR a short numbered list of discrepancies, identifying what the certificate says, the correction requested and the supporting document. For example: “The start date shown is 1 August; my appointment and first payslip record 1 July. Please check and issue a corrected certificate if appropriate.”

Retain the original and the response. Ask for a replacement issued by the employer rather than editing the PDF yourself. Keep the corrected version clearly identified so an old copy is not accidentally sent with a job application.

If it has not been issued

Write to HR using a contact you can retain after work-email access ends. Include your employment period, employee reference if relevant, the request for a certificate of service and a safe delivery method. Keep evidence of the request and follow-up.

If the employer refuses or does not resolve the issue, take the documents to a labour officer, union representative or qualified employment adviser. Ask about the procedure and deadlines for your circumstances. Do not assume a generic online letter guarantees a particular outcome.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 10 November 2026. Employment Act sections 51 support the legal points above. The practical checklists are editorial guidance; examples are illustrative.

title: Salary Review Letters: What to Check
featuredImageAlt: Professional reading a plain salary-review letter beside a calculator and coral notebook
metaTitle: Salary Review Letters: What to Check
metaDescription: Check a salary review letter in Kenya: basic versus gross pay, effective dates, allowances, arrears and the first revised payslip, with a worked example.
content:
Before payroll implements a salary review, confirm the new recurring amount, what it includes, the effective date and the first payment date. A letter announcing a percentage increase can still leave payroll uncertain about the figure to enter.

Use the pay rise calculator after establishing the old and new comparable gross salaries. For the tax arithmetic, read how much of a pay rise you keep. This checklist concerns the written instruction behind the change.

Identify the amount being reviewed

Check whether the letter refers to basic pay, total gross cash pay, net pay or the employer's total package cost. Ask for a breakdown if it does not say. Employer contributions and non-cash benefits should not silently be treated as cash salary.

Write down the old basic salary, each recurring allowance and the corresponding new amounts. Ask which items are unchanged. A higher basic salary accompanied by an absorbed allowance can produce a smaller increase in total cash pay than the headline suggests.

Section 10(5) of the Employment Act requires consultation, revision of the contract to reflect changes to the relevant employment particulars and written notification. Keep the confirmed letter with the employment terms; a payroll entry alone is not a useful record of what was agreed.

Example: a 10% increase to basic salary

Suppose basic pay is KES 60,000 and a separate recurring allowance is KES 10,000. If the confirmed review increases only basic pay by 10% and leaves the allowance unchanged, the new basic is KES 66,000 and gross cash pay is KES 76,000.

The total increase is KES 6,000 from a previous KES 70,000 gross, or about 8.57%. Entering KES 77,000 would incorrectly apply 10% to the whole former gross amount. These are illustrative contract figures, not a statement that any employee is entitled to an annual 10% rise.

Check the gross versus net salary explanation if the employer promises an amount “after tax”. Obtain a clear definition of which deductions are included in that promise before using it in a calculation.

Separate the effective date from the payment date

A letter may be signed in November but state that the change takes effect in October. Ask whether November's payslip will show both the new recurring salary and a separately identified adjustment for October.

Record the months covered and the old and new rates for each. Follow the salary arrears checklist for a backdated change; do not treat every earlier-period adjustment as an ordinary bonus. If the change starts mid-month, request the agreed proration basis rather than inventing a divisor.

Check related terms explicitly

Ask whether the change affects pensionable pay, commission targets, overtime calculations or benefits. Do not assume every component automatically tracks basic salary. Where a percentage contribution is involved, identify both the percentage and the pay base.

If a one-off award accompanies the increase, keep it separate from the recurring salary. A large first revised payment can otherwise create an unrealistic expectation of next month's cash. The salary breakdown guide helps interpret those separate lines.

Reconcile the first revised payslip

Compare the letter with earnings before checking deductions. KRA's PAYE guidance uses progressive income-tax bands; the gross increase is not the same as the extra bank credit. Use the calculator with consistent assumptions and ask payroll about benefit changes or personal deductions that affect the comparison.

Send a focused query if the amount is wrong: identify the confirmed effective date, expected earnings line and actual payslip line. Keep payroll's correction and the revised document. Review the following month as well to ensure a one-off adjustment has not accidentally become recurring salary.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 10 November 2026. Employment Act sections 10(5) support the legal points above. The practical checklists are editorial guidance; examples are illustrative.

Employment Act: Ministry of Labour official copy. KRA PAYE guidance.

title: Payroll Loan Balance: Checks Before Leaving a Job
metaTitle: Payroll Loan Balance: Checks Before Leaving a Job
metaDescription: Leaving a Kenyan job with a payroll loan? Reconcile deductions, lender credits, interest and the settlement quote before agreeing the final recovery.
featuredImageAlt: Employee comparing two plain paper records beside a calculator, coral notebook and work bag
content:
Before leaving a job with an outstanding payroll loan, reconcile three records: the loan agreement, deductions on your payslips and credits on the lender's statement. A figure on an exit clearance form is a starting point, not a substitute for that reconciliation.

Use the PAYE calculator to check ordinary salary deductions before considering loan recovery. It cannot determine your loan balance or the amount legally recoverable from a particular final settlement. The employment situations guide covers the wider payroll changes when a job ends.

Identify who lent the money

Confirm whether the creditor is your employer, a bank, a SACCO or another lender. Payroll may only collect the instalment for someone else. Record the loan reference, original amount, repayment terms and the party responsible for issuing a settlement statement.

Keep a salary advance separate from a longer-term loan. Our salary advance explanation deals with early payment and later recovery of salary. This checklist concerns the remaining debt and the handover from payroll collection when employment ends.

Reconcile principal, interest and actual credits

Ask for a statement through an agreed cut-off date. Start with the opening principal, add further borrowing and subtract the principal portion of repayments. Track interest and charges separately, using the agreement and the lender's allocation of each instalment. Subtracting every payslip deduction from principal can understate the balance if part paid interest.

Create one row per repayment with the payroll month, deduction date, amount withheld, remittance reference, lender credit date and allocation. Mark differences as unresolved rather than inserting an unexplained balancing figure. A missing credit may involve timing, an incorrect reference or an unremitted deduction; establish which before paying the same instalment again.

Worked example: why the last payslip matters

Suppose opening principal is KES 80,000. Two instalments of KES 12,000 each are split, under the lender's statement, into KES 10,000 principal and KES 2,000 interest. After both credits, principal is KES 60,000, not KES 56,000.

If the statement shows only the first instalment, it will show KES 70,000 principal. The second KES 12,000 payroll deduction needs tracing. Send its remittance reference to the lender and request an updated statement. Do not simply pay the quoted KES 70,000 while treating the second deduction as lost.

These are illustrative allocations, not a recommended loan rate. A dated settlement quote may also include accrued interest or agreed charges, so it can differ from the principal balance. Request an itemised explanation and the date through which the quote is valid.

Check final-pay recovery separately

Employment Act section 19(1)(h) addresses repayment of an employer loan under a written agreement and limits that deduction to 50% of wages remaining after other deductions under the section. Section 19(3) separately limits total wage deductions to two-thirds, subject to any other prescribed amount, without extinguishing debt-recovery rights.

Those provisions are not permission to take every item in a terminal settlement. Ask payroll to identify the authority, wage base, other deductions and proposed recovery. The salary deduction guide explains why authority and amount need separate checks. Obtain advice from a labour officer or qualified adviser if the proposed recovery is disputed.

Keep the final earnings and PAYE calculation separate from the debt settlement schedule. A loan repayment is not automatically an allowable PAYE deduction. Our employee exit payroll checklist helps reconcile the rest of the final payment.

Agree what happens after the last payroll

  1. Confirm the last payroll instalment and whether the lender has credited it.
  2. Get written instructions for any balance, payment channel, due dates and reference after departure.
  3. Check whether leaving changes interest, instalments or repayment timing under the agreement; do not assume the old payroll arrangement continues.
  4. After settlement, obtain the final statement and confirmation that payroll deductions have stopped.
  5. Retain the agreement, payslips, remittance evidence and settlement confirmation together.

A clearance signature and a zero loan balance answer different questions. Close the query only when the records explain both the amount recovered from your pay and what remains due to the lender.

Sources and review date

Published and reviewed 11 November 2026. Legal reference: Employment Act, section 19, Ministry of Labour copy. Tax framework: KRA PAYE guidance and allowable deductions. Reconciliation steps and figures are editorial examples, not a ruling on an individual settlement.

title: Salary Sacrifice in Kenya: Check the Proposal
metaTitle: Salary Sacrifice in Kenya: Check the Proposal
metaDescription: Review a salary sacrifice proposal in Kenya: compare cash, taxable benefits, deductions and contract changes without assuming an automatic tax saving.
featuredImageAlt: Two professionals comparing plain proposal sheets with a calculator and coral folder
content:
If an employer proposes replacing some cash salary with a benefit or contribution, ask for two complete payroll illustrations before agreeing. The term “salary sacrifice” describes the proposed exchange; it does not establish how Kenyan tax rules apply to that exchange.

Start with the salary comparison calculator to compare the cash-salary baselines. A benefit arrangement needs payroll's specific valuation and deduction treatment as well. The salary breakdown guide explains how the earnings and deduction lines fit together.

Write down what is being exchanged

Ask for the current cash salary, the amount being surrendered, the replacement benefit, who pays the provider and when the arrangement begins. Establish whether the proposal changes contractual gross pay or merely adds a deduction from pay already earned. Those are different payroll instructions.

Record the cost to the employer, the value used for tax and the value to you separately. A benefit priced at KES 10,000 is not necessarily worth KES 10,000 in cash to your household. Keep any employee co-payment visible too, so it is not accidentally charged both as a salary reduction and as a second deduction.

Ask for the Kenyan tax basis for each line

KRA's PAYE guidance includes cash remuneration and taxable non-cash benefits, while identifying particular exclusions and allowable deductions. The relevant treatment depends on the benefit or contribution and its conditions. An overseas salary-sacrifice example does not establish a Kenyan exemption.

Request the applicable rule, benefit valuation, any limit and the evidence payroll needs. For pension funding, identify whether it is an employee contribution or an employer contribution. For cover, distinguish an employer-provided policy from cash paid to buy one. Do not assume each route produces the same payroll result.

Read the benefits-in-kind guide for classification, and salary versus benefits for valuing the non-cash part. This article focuses on checking an exchange within an existing remuneration arrangement.

Reconcile cash pay and taxable pay separately

Build a before-and-after worksheet containing gross cash pay, taxable benefit value, qualifying deductions, PAYE, each statutory contribution, other cash deductions and final bank payment. Ask payroll to explain each changed line. Never assume that reducing cash salary reduces every contribution base by exactly the same amount.

A useful arithmetic check is cash earnings less cash deductions equals the bank payment. A non-cash benefit can enter the tax calculation without becoming money payable to your bank. An employer's contribution should not silently appear as an employee cash receipt.

Example: a taxable benefit can replace the surrendered cash

Assume current monthly cash pay is KES 100,000, with no taxable benefit. A proposal replaces KES 10,000 cash with a benefit that payroll has separately confirmed has a taxable value of KES 10,000. Proposed cash is KES 90,000, but cash plus taxable benefit remains KES 100,000 before allowable deductions.

It would be wrong to calculate PAYE from KES 90,000 while omitting that confirmed benefit. If allowable deductions and reliefs were unchanged, the taxable amount and PAYE would be unchanged too. The exact bank-payment difference still needs all contribution and deduction lines checked.

This is a classification example, not a valuation rule for a car, home, pension or medical policy. If the actual benefit is exempt, has a different statutory valuation or changes eligible deductions, payroll must redo the comparison with those facts.

Check the contract and the exit terms

Employment Act section 10(5) requires consultation, revision of the contract and written notification when the relevant employment particulars change. Ask for the agreed terms before the new payroll entry starts.

  • Is the change temporary, and how can it be reversed?
  • What happens if the benefit provider fails to supply the service?
  • Which salary figure will be used for future percentage reviews and pensionable pay?
  • What happens on unpaid leave or departure, including any remaining provider payments?
  • Are there fees, minimum periods or restrictions that reduce the benefit's usefulness?

Keep the answers with the proposal. Avoid accepting an estimate headed “tax saving” without the full cash comparison, and do not count inaccessible retirement savings as money available for monthly bills.

Verify the first month and the ongoing month

Compare the first payslip with the signed terms and both illustrations. Look for a benefit starting before the salary change, a repeated co-payment or a one-off provider fee. Then check the next normal month; implementation adjustments can make the first month unrepresentative.

Sources and review date

Published and reviewed 11 November 2026. Sources: KRA PAYE guidance and Employment Act section 10(5). The worksheet and example are editorial checks, not confirmation that a proposed scheme qualifies for tax relief.

title: Payroll Name and KRA PIN Mismatches: What to Check
metaTitle: Payroll Name and KRA PIN Mismatches: What to Check
metaDescription: Resolve a Kenyan payroll name or KRA PIN mismatch by locating the wrong record, using KRA correction guidance and checking payslips, returns and your P9.
featuredImageAlt: Payroll professional checking a blank grid sheet beside a coral employee folder and closed laptop
content:
A misspelled name on a payslip and an incorrect KRA PIN in a PAYE return are different problems. Start by identifying which record is wrong. Changing a payroll display name does not, by itself, correct KRA's registration record or a return already filed.

The PAYE calculator helps check the salary arithmetic once the employee's circumstances are established. It cannot validate a PIN or confirm where tax was recorded. Use the employer payroll guide alongside this record-correction checklist.

Compare the records without guessing

Gather the employee's current KRA PIN certificate, relevant identity document, payroll profile and affected payslip or P9. Use the employer's secure document channel. Compare the PIN character by character and distinguish the employee PIN from the employer PIN.

Record where the discrepancy appears: only the printed payslip, the underlying employee record, the tax certificate or a filed return. Ask payroll to confirm what it actually submitted, rather than assuming the displayed name proves the return is correct or incorrect.

A difference in name order may need clarification rather than replacement of the identifier. An apparent one-character PIN typo still needs checking against the certificate; do not infer the right character or borrow another employee's record as a template.

If only the employer's record is wrong

Send payroll a specific correction request: the affected field, the verified replacement, the supporting document and the earliest affected month. Ask a reviewer to confirm the change in the employee master record and any separate payroll export used for returns.

Request a corrected payslip or P9 where appropriate, retaining the earlier version with a clear note that it has been superseded. Updating next month's template alone can leave an incorrect year-end certificate in circulation.

The new employee payroll checklist is useful for preventing a repeat. Include a second check when records are copied into a new payroll system or imported from a spreadsheet.

If KRA's registration details are wrong

KRA's registration data correction notice describes the iTax route through Registration, Amend PIN details, using online amendment and supporting documents where required. Its registration FAQ specifically directs taxpayers with misspelled names to KRA's contact centre with their PIN and colour scans of the original identity document.

Use the current official guidance for the field you need changed. If the name cannot be edited, or your PIN is linked to a passport, ask KRA for the applicable process rather than forcing an unrelated amendment. The FAQ flags a limitation for passport-linked name amendments. Keep the enquiry or application reference and follow through until KRA confirms the outcome.

Navigate from KRA's official website and verify the recipient before sending identity documents. Payroll needs the corrected record, not your iTax password or one-time security code. Do not register another PIN merely to work around a mismatch.

If a return has already used the wrong details

Ask the employer to list the affected return periods and entries. The correction may involve more than changing your personal profile. Payroll should establish the proper return-correction route and reconcile the submitted records with KRA where necessary.

Use the PAYE return correction checklist to assemble the evidence. Do not assume that a corrected name automatically moves a tax payment, or that a fresh deduction is the appropriate remedy for a reporting error.

Example: correct tax arithmetic, wrong identifier

Suppose three payslips each show KES 8,000 PAYE, and the employer confirms that all three return entries used an incorrect employee PIN. The KES 24,000 total identifies the amount to reconcile; it does not prove that the employee should pay another KES 24,000 or that the existing tax has already been reassigned.

Build a three-row schedule with month, payslip deduction, submitted identifier, correct identifier and correction status. Add references to the employer's submission and payment evidence. Ask for confirmation of the corrected treatment for each month and a consistent P9. The figures illustrate the record problem, not the tax on a particular salary.

Close the query across all affected records

  • Check KRA's confirmed registration details where those were amended.
  • Check the next payslip and the employer's payroll profile.
  • Confirm the outcome for each earlier affected return period.
  • Match the final P9 to the corrected payroll totals.
  • Retain the correspondence and correction references for annual reconciliation.

Our P9 reconciliation guide helps with that last comparison. A screenshot showing the new name is useful evidence of one change; it is not a complete check of every affected tax record.

Sources and review date

Published and reviewed 11 November 2026. Official sources: KRA taxpayer registration data correction notice and KRA registration FAQs. The reconciliation workflow is editorial guidance. No processing time or automatic transfer of tax credits is promised.

title: Sick Pay and PAYE in Kenya
metaTitle: Sick Pay and PAYE in Kenya
metaDescription: Check sick-pay entitlement, half-pay calculations and PAYE on your Kenyan payslip, with a practical example and steps for correcting payroll errors.
content:
Sick pay in Kenya is employment income for PAYE. Being away from work because of illness does not, by itself, make the salary paid during that absence tax-free. First check how much sick pay you are entitled to; then check the deductions from that amount.

Use the Kenya PAYE calculator with the confirmed gross pay for the affected month to estimate take-home pay. The calculator does not decide your sick-leave entitlement or the correct daily rate under your contract.

Which sick-pay entitlement applies?

Section 30 of the Employment Act provides a minimum after two consecutive months of service: seven days on full pay followed by seven on half pay in each twelve-month service period. Medical certification and prompt notification of the absence are required. Check the applicable wage order, collective agreement and contract for more favourable terms; do not assume seven days is your entire entitlement.

For example, paragraph 12 of the Regulation of Wages (General) Order provides up to thirty days on full pay and then fifteen on half pay after two months of continuous service, subject to its conditions. Its application provisions exclude agricultural workers. This is why payroll must identify the rules covering your employment before moving you to half pay.

Ask HR to identify the rule it used and provide your opening sick-leave balance, days already used and the dates now charged. Confirm the employer's leave-year cycle. A payroll code labelled “absence” is not enough to establish whether a day should be paid, half-paid or unpaid.

Is there a separate sick-pay tax rate?

No separate sick-pay rate is listed in KRA's PAYE guidance on employment income. Sick pay joins the other taxable employment payments in the payroll calculation. Full pay is not a promise that the whole gross amount reaches your bank account: lawful deductions can still apply.

If gross pay falls during a half-pay period, payroll should calculate the month from the revised earnings and applicable deductions. Do not simply halve last month's net salary or PAYE. See why taxable pay differs from gross pay before comparing the tax line.

A half-pay example you can reconcile

Suppose payroll has confirmed that five days are payable at half the normal daily rate of KES 2,000. Normal pay for those five days would be KES 10,000; half pay is KES 5,000. The reduction in gross earnings is therefore KES 5,000, not KES 10,000.

If the otherwise unchanged month's gross earnings would have been KES 60,000, the revised gross is KES 55,000. This example assumes the rate, affected days and treatment of other earnings have already been agreed. It does not prescribe a universal divisor for monthly salaries or determine an allowance entitlement. Ask payroll to show its actual daily-rate calculation.

Enter KES 55,000 into the calculator for a standard salary estimate, then account for your own pension, reliefs and other deductions. The KES 5,000 gross reduction is not automatically a KES 5,000 reduction in take-home pay.

What to check on the payslip

  • Match the absence dates to the approved leave record and medical certificate.
  • Separate full-pay days, half-pay days and any disputed unpaid days.
  • Check that a gross salary reduction has not also been collected as a second net-pay deduction.
  • Compare taxable pay, PAYE and each other deduction separately with the previous payslip.
  • Ask how a late certificate or correction will appear in the next payroll and whether earlier records need correcting.

Use the payslip reading checklist to identify the relevant lines. Send payroll a short dated query stating the disputed days, rate and amount, with supporting records through the employer's secure channel. Keep the response and corrected payslip.

What if the absence lasts longer?

Request written confirmation of the next period's leave classification and pay before assuming it is paid or unpaid. The answer depends on the applicable entitlement and remaining balance. A medical insurance benefit and salary continuation are different questions; ask separately about cover and pay. Our employment situations guide connects the other payroll issues that may arise.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 12 November 2026 against the Employment Act, section 30, and KRA's employment-income guidance linked above. Examples are illustrative payroll reconciliations, not determinations of a particular employee's entitlement.

title: Maternity Pay and PAYE in Kenya
metaTitle: Maternity Pay and PAYE in Kenya
metaDescription: Understand maternity pay, PAYE and payslip checks in Kenya, including leave dates, annual leave and how to question an unexpected salary reduction.
content:
Maternity leave with full pay does not mean maternity pay is exempt from PAYE in Kenya. The leave entitlement determines the pay due; the payroll calculation then determines deductions and take-home pay. Confirm both before budgeting for your leave.

Use the Kenya PAYE calculator to estimate an ordinary month's take-home from your confirmed gross salary. It cannot decide disputed benefits or whether an additional period of leave is paid.

What does the maternity-leave entitlement cover?

Section 29 of the Employment Act provides three months of maternity leave with full pay. Give written notice at least seven days ahead, or a shorter reasonable period in the circumstances; a medical certificate may be requested. Taking maternity leave does not forfeit annual leave. The Act also protects return to the same or a reasonably suitable job on no less favourable terms.

Before leave starts, ask HR to confirm the start date, expected return date, payroll contact and how you will receive payslips. Check the contract and any applicable collective agreement for better terms. Record any agreed additional leave separately, including its pay basis; an extension should not be assumed to carry the same pay automatically.

Why PAYE can still appear during maternity leave

KRA includes salary and leave pay in employment income. Salary continuing during maternity leave therefore remains within the PAYE calculation. The fact that you are not attending work is not a general tax exemption.

Compare like with like. If ordinary gross pay, taxable benefits, eligible reliefs and deductions are unchanged, the leave label alone should not change the salary calculation. An unusual take-home amount needs a line-by-line explanation rather than an assumption that maternity leave attracts a special tax rate. Read gross versus net salary to separate contractual pay from the bank transfer.

A simple example: relabelling is not extra salary

Suppose your confirmed monthly gross salary during leave is KES 80,000, with no additional cash earnings. One payroll system may show KES 80,000 as basic salary; another may show it under a maternity-pay code. The total cash earnings should still be KES 80,000. Adding KES 80,000 maternity pay on top of the same KES 80,000 salary would incorrectly produce KES 160,000 unless a genuine additional payment was due.

Likewise, moving to an approved maternity-leave code should not silently turn the salary line to zero. Ask for the pay calculation if the system shows both an unpaid-absence deduction and full maternity pay. Check the total rather than relying on the label.

Checks before leave and on the first payslip

  • Keep the written notice, HR acknowledgement and confirmed leave dates.
  • Obtain a breakdown of continuing salary and benefits, including any variable earnings whose treatment needs explanation.
  • Confirm how existing pension contributions, loan repayments and other payroll arrangements will be handled; ask about each rather than assuming they stop.
  • Check gross earnings, taxable pay, reliefs, PAYE and net pay on the first leave-month payslip.
  • Compare the net-pay figure with the amount received and retain any explanation of a correction.

If tax looks wrong, use the steps for querying incorrect PAYE. If gross earnings are wrong, ask HR to resolve the leave coding and pay entitlement first; recalculating tax alone will not fix missing salary.

Annual leave and the return-to-work payroll

Ask HR to show maternity leave and any annual leave as separate entries in the leave record. Confirm the agreed return date again if plans change, then inspect the first return-month payslip for duplicate absence reductions, delayed adjustments or missed salary changes. Preserve the earlier payslips so that a catch-up payment can be traced to its period.

The employment situations guide covers related payroll changes. For an unresolved entitlement dispute, take the written records to a labour officer or a qualified adviser; a calculator can estimate deductions but cannot settle the employment dispute.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 12 November 2026 using Employment Act section 29 and KRA's employment-income guidance linked above. The example explains payroll presentation and does not quote a personalised net salary.

title: Changing Payroll Systems: Kenya Migration Checks
metaTitle: Changing Payroll Systems: Kenya Migration Checks
metaDescription: Move Kenyan payroll systems with checks for opening balances, employee records, PAYE exports and parallel runs before authorising the first payment.
content:
When a Kenyan employer changes payroll systems, the most useful test is whether the same approved inputs produce an explainable payroll in both systems. A successful import message is not evidence that employee balances, deductions or return files are correct.

Use the employer cost calculator as an independent check of standard gross salary and employer-cost components. It is a baseline check, not a replacement for validating every employee's benefits, reliefs and deductions in the new system.

Agree the cutover month and preserve the old records

Name the final period processed in the old system and the first period in the new one. Record who can approve imports, payroll changes, payment files and statutory submissions. Keep a read-only export of the final approved payroll, employee master data, year-to-date totals, payslips and outstanding balances before changing anything.

Build an import register showing the source field, destination field, conversion rule and reviewer. Pay special attention to dates, decimal places, employee numbers and identifiers stored with leading zeros. Follow the broader payroll record checklist when deciding what must remain accessible after the old subscription ends.

Reconcile opening balances by employee

Compare employee counts and totals first, then investigate individual differences. A matching grand total can hide two employees' balances being swapped. Use a stable employee reference alongside the name and relevant statutory identifiers.

  • Reconcile year-to-date earnings, taxable amounts, PAYE and relief records to the approved monthly history.
  • Transfer loan and advance balances with their repayment instructions and end dates.
  • Carry forward leave balances with the correct leave type and period.
  • Check recurring allowances, taxable benefits, voluntary deductions and employer contributions separately.
  • Keep joiners, leavers and employees on leave in the correct status, without reviving ended deductions.

For example, a loan opens at KES 36,000 and an authorised KES 6,000 instalment is deducted in the first new-system month. The closing principal should be KES 30,000 if there are no other principal movements. Importing KES 30,000 as the opening balance and deducting again would incorrectly leave KES 24,000. Preserve the balance date as well as the amount.

Run the same payroll in both systems before payment

Use one agreed set of inputs for a parallel test run. Compare gross earnings, taxable benefits, allowed deductions, reliefs, PAYE, net pay and employer costs. Include ordinary salaries and real edge cases: a joiner, a leaver, a benefit recipient, a salary adjustment and an employee whose recurring deduction has ended.

Investigate every material difference. Separate a corrected old configuration from a new import error and a documented rounding difference. Do not force the new system to reproduce an old mistake simply to make totals match. Record the reason and approval for any intentional difference.

Validate return and payment exports separately

KRA's simplified PAYE-return notice directs employers to its Excel return and sample CSVs, with full rollout from 1 July 2025. Check the current official template when configuring the export. A vendor's claim that a file is “iTax ready” should still be tested against the relevant fields and totals.

Reconcile the return output with the approved payroll, then reconcile the bank-payment total with net pay. Prevent test files from being released as payments or filed as real returns. Changing software does not restart tax periods or remove existing obligations: KRA's PAYE obligations page explains the employer's deduction and remittance duty.

If identifier errors appear, use the name and KRA PIN mismatch checks to distinguish a master-data correction from an already-filed return issue. Avoid silently rewriting historical submissions during migration.

Approve the first live run and give employees a comparison

Obtain sign-off on opening balances, unresolved exceptions, the first live payroll and the files actually released. Keep a recovery plan that identifies the last approved data and who can stop a duplicate payment. After payment, reconcile the bank result and statutory acknowledgements back to the authorised run.

Tell employees when the payslip layout changes and where to raise discrepancies. An employee should be able to compare old and new gross pay, deductions and net pay even if the labels differ. The employer payroll guide provides the wider monthly workflow; these migration controls focus on preserving continuity between systems.

Sources and review date

Reviewed 12 November 2026. Official KRA sources are linked above. The migration sequence and balance example are practical editorial controls, not a claim that KRA certifies a particular payroll product.
